## EDA
For initial, brief EDA look into the $starter.r$ file, where I explain my thoughts in comments.

## DAG
My DAG looks like this:
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
library(dagitty)
dag <- dagitty(" dag{
               age -> alcohol
               age -> speeding
               age -> ksi
               night -> alcohol
               night -> speeding
               night -> ksi
               alcohol -> ksi
               alcohol -> seat_belt
               alcohol -> speeding
               alcohol -> blood_test
               seat_belt -> ksi
               speeding -> ksi
               ksi -> blood_test
}")

plot(dag)
```
Here is the reasoning behind it: people tend to drink more in the evnings, also speeding is easier in the night with empty roads, also nighttime accidents tend to be more severe. Younger drivers tend to speed more (put a lil joke how a is_bmw column would be beneficial), and middle aged men tend to drunk drive the most, while older drivers are quicker to fall victim to injuries. Alcohol affects seat belt usage and speeding, as well as a blood test, because for a blood test to be "yes", there was definetely alcohol present. We also draw an edge from alcohol to ksi as this is the link we are interested in. Also ksi affects blood test as blood test is administered when a driver cannot take the breathalizer test.

Confounders(affect both alcohol and ksi):

* night
* age

Mediators(on the causal path from alcohol to ksi):

* seat belt
* speeding

Collider(common effect of two variables that you must not adjust for because conditioning on it creates spurious bias):

* blood_test

Using adjustmentSets() on the DAG, it said I should use night and age variable to infer a TOTAL effect of alcohol on ksi - so only include variables that link TO alcohol. 

You include age and night not just because they point to alcohol, but because they are confounders—they have paths leading to both alcohol and ksi (creating open "backdoor" paths that would bias your estimate if left unadjusted).


## Binomial regression model
To answer the question: How much more likely is a driver with alcohol to be killed or seriously injured in an accident compared to a sober driver?

We are interested if ksi event is true for each accident and to compare the numbers for alcohol present and not present - this would use a bernoulli distribution. But because our data is aggregated we are using binomial distribution to model the number of successes (a bit morbid since these are ksi) woth probability p in a fixed number of independent trials (accidents, number means drivers).

One small nuance you can save for your Discussion/Limitations section later: two drivers involved in the exact same multi-car crash aren't strictly independent, so treating all drivers as independent trials is a modeling approximation—a very standard and reasonable one here, but worth noting.
